title: Feng Shui for Homes from an Architect's View: What to Keep, What to Skip
desc: Many feng shui beliefs match good architecture: breezes, daylight, a clear entrance. How to balance feng shui with function, safety and building regulations.
summary: An analysis of common feng shui beliefs for homes from an architectural view: which have sound reasons and are worth keeping, and which should not be traded against function, safety and legal compliance.
body: p

When building, many families care a great deal about feng shui: door direction, kitchen position, staircase, number of steps… This article does not debate the truth of beliefs, but looks at common ideas from an architectural angle: many are in fact good lived experience handed down by our forebears, but some, if followed rigidly, will make the house less convenient and less safe.
h2
1. Where feng shui and architecture “say the same thing”
ul

A house that catches breezes and has enough light (“storing wind, gathering qi”): in architectural terms this is natural ventilation and good lighting – a house that is cool, dry and less prone to damp and mould.
A clear, bright entrance: guests find it easily, security is better, and exit is quick in an emergency.

Avoiding a front door looking straight through to the back door: architecturally, strong drafts rush through the house and privacy is lacking; a screen or half-height partition can redirect the airflow.
A kitchen not facing or adjoining the toilet: sensible for hygiene, odour and plumbing.
Quiet, private bedrooms: avoid placing them right next to the stairs, the street or the parking area.
h2
2. Where function should not be traded away
ul
Counting stair steps by the “birth – ageing – sickness – death” cycle: if forcing the step count makes risers uneven, it is easy to cause falls. Safety matters more than the number.
Turning the front door off-axis to match an age and so narrowing the entrance, blocking the escape route or making it hard to bring a vehicle into the house.
Dimensions by the Lu Ban ruler: can be consulted when choosing doors and the altar, but must not make door sizes and escape routes too small.
Placing water tanks and septic tanks in “suitable” positions that are far from drainage, hard to pump out and hard to maintain.
h2
3. Feng shui does not replace building regulations
p
However well a building suits feng shui, it must still comply with the rules:
ul
Do not build beyond the height and distances set by construction law, and do not infringe the rights of adjoining houses (Article 174 of the Civil Code).

Do not encroach on, occupy or alter boundary markers; land boundaries must be respected (Article 175). Windows, balconies and roofs must not cross the plot boundary into the neighbour's (section 2.5.8 of QCVN 01:2026/BXD, effective from 1 January 2027).
Rainwater from the roof must not flow onto the neighbour's house (Article 250).
The facade, colours and projecting parts must follow the planning and the architectural management regulations where you build.
p

Things such as a “bagua mirror aimed at the house opposite” or building much higher than the neighbour to “suppress” them should be reconsidered because they easily cause neighbour conflicts. For construction-related disputes see also Building causes a neighbour's house to settle or crack: liability and compensation.
h2
4. How to reconcile them when working with an architect
ol
State clearly from the start the feng shui requirements most important to your family (usually the front door direction, the altar position and the kitchen).
Let the architect propose options that meet those requirements while still ensuring light, ventilation, circulation and safety.
For minor requirements, accept “remedies” through interior elements (partitions, plants, colours) rather than changing the structure.
Settle the scheme before applying for the permit and building; changes midway are costly and may require adjusting the permit.
h2
5. Groundbreaking date and ceremony
p

Choosing an auspicious date is a custom for many families. Legally, what matters is that before starting construction the required conditions are in place, such as the construction permit (if required), the design and the contract with the contractor – see Conditions for starting construction of a house.
p

note
